facts.text: Run by City Grazing, a San Francisco nonprofit that uses goat grazing for land management.
Beach Blanket Babylon played here for 45 years, from 1974.
The Grateful Dead held their first album release party here in 1967.
Thelonious Monk recorded Thelonious Alone in San Francisco here in 1959.
Founded in 1982 as Cobb's Pub on Chestnut Street in the Marina District.
Moved to the Cannery at Fisherman's Wharf in 1987, then to Columbus Avenue in 2002 after a fire.
Operated as 848 Performance Space from 1991 to 2005 before becoming CounterPulse.
Opened at its Turk Street home in spring 2016 through a lease-to-purchase with the Community Arts Stabilization Trust.
Named after Homer Curran, who partnered with Shubert Incorporated to build it.
Reopened in January 2017 with Fun Home after a major restoration.

name: Cutting Ball Theater
note: KQED farewell article and SF Chronicle 'Cutting Ball Theater is closing' (search result titles) say the company ceased operations at end of 2024.

name: Diego Rivera Theatre
note: Matched at CCSF Ocean Campus; new Diego Rivera Performing Arts Center broke ground Jan 2026, no single-page fact tied.

facts.text: Intersection for the Arts ran the building as a theater from 1990 to 2011.
Ty Mckenzie ran it as Stage Werx from 2012 until handing it to the Eclectic Box collective in 2023.
The building was Mancuso Brothers Furniture Store for almost sixty years.
An improv comedy theater that also teaches a five-level core improv curriculum.

name: Founders Amphitheatre
note: Located at Southeast Community Center (1550 Evans Ave); no result tied to Founders Amphitheatre name by a single page.

facts.text: 42nd Street Moon took over the lease after the venue was renamed the Gateway Theatre.
Designed by G. Albert Lansburgh for the Radio-Keith-Orpheum circuit and opened as a vaudeville house.
Closed in 1972 and was reopened as a performing arts venue in 1979.
Opened in 1925 as the Great China Theatre, built for Chinese opera.
An indoor trampoline park in a historic former airplane hangar in the Presidio.
A Greek-style amphitheater in McLaren Park that opened in 1971.
Named for Jerry Garcia by the Recreation and Park Commission in 2005.

name: John A. and Cynthia Fry Gunn Theater

facts.text: A theater inside the Legion of Honor museum in Lincoln Park.
Built in 1928; it was renamed Cinema 21 in 1965 and reopened in 2008 as a two-screen second-floor theater.
Built in 1926 as part of the Marines' Memorial Club building.
Former home of the Actors Workshop and the American Conservatory Theatre.

name: Nourse Theater
note: Now named the Sydney Goldstein Theater (renamed after the OSM name); still open.

facts.text: Opened in 1926 as a high school auditorium and reopened in 2013 as a home for City Arts & Lectures.
Now called the Sydney Goldstein Theater.
Founded by Brenda Way of ODC and a presenter of dance and performance since 1976.
Operated by Landmark Theatres since 1991 and reopened in November 2021 after a renovation.
Pre-Broadway runs here included Evita and Mamma Mia!
The Palace of Fine Arts Theatre opened in 1970, after the Palace of Fine Arts League formed in 1962 to restore the Palace.
The Palace was designed by Bernard Maybeck for the 1915 Panama-Pacific International Exposition.
A 99-seat venue run by PlayGround that was founded by Thick Description as Thick House in 1999.
Reopened in 2017 as Potrero Stage after a 2016 renovation.

name: Presidio Dance Theatre
note: Press page says the company moved from its old home near Doyle Drive to the Presidio Performing Arts Center on the Main Post (2011); OSM point is the old location.
